evidence.note: Cherry-picked SCHED-order-knob commits 17f599aab (order+order_pin knob) and 3db982a8d (layered-knob merge helper) onto ddflow/fix-B0db4e156e8; added order/order_pin knobs to ScheduleConfig, effective_order() in _filters.py, 4 listed=False keys, regression test test_schedule_order_knob.py (13 pass).

chunk_findings.detail: `_pin_problem` validates `order_pin` with `last_id=False`, so it accepts `id` as a pinned key, and `merge_pin` then unconditionally places pinned keys at the head and removes them from the base. For example, with the default `order = ["recover_first", "bugs_first", "unphased_first", "priority", "id"]` and a config setting `order_pin = ["id"]`, validation passes, but `merge_pin` returns `["id", "recover_first", "bugs_first", "unphased_first", "priority"]`. That makes `id` the primary ordering key and removes the documented deterministic tie-break at the end; if `effective_order` later moves `id` back to last instead, the documented “pinned to the HEAD” behavior is silently ignored. Either way, `order_pin` can produce an order that violates the `order` knob’s stated invariant that `id` must be last.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/schedule.py:_pin_problem / merge_pin

chunk_findings.detail: Given a config where `[schedule].order_pin` contains `"id"` (for example `order_pin = ["id", "priority"]` and `order` is the default), `effective_order` copies `sched.order_pin` verbatim, removes `"id"` only from `base`, and then appends `"id"` again. It returns something like `["id", "priority", ..., "id"]`. The resulting `order_key` therefore compares `id` before `priority`, so a lower item id outranks priority, contradicting the function's documented invariant that `id` is last and the usual tiebreak semantics.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/schedule/_filters.py:effective_order

chunk_findings.detail: The `order` row states that `id` is always last (“appended when omitted, refused elsewhere”), while the new `order_pin` row states that keys are pinned to the head of the order, ahead of `order`, with no exception for `id`. If a user sets `schedule.order_pin = ["id"]`, the documentation simultaneously says `id` must be placed first and that `id` may only appear last. This makes the configuration contract ambiguous: either the code must reject `id` in `order_pin` and the docs omit that restriction, or the documented always-last invariant can be violated.
chunk_findings.title: docs/guide/parallelism.md:312-313

chunk_findings.detail: The retry loop does not enforce `record_lock_wait_s` as a total wait. It sets `deadline = time.monotonic() + wait_s`, but then calls `log.append`, which can block for the full `[lease].acquire_timeout_s`, and only checks the deadline after that attempt has already timed out. With `[lease].record_lock_wait_s = 1`, `[lease].acquire_timeout_s = 30`, and the events lock held by a lane heartbeat, `_append_outcome` will block for roughly 30 seconds before raising `AppendLockTimeout`, even though the knob documentation says `wait_s` bounds the total wait across attempts. More generally, the actual total wait can exceed the configured `record_lock_wait_s` by up to one full `acquire_timeout_s` (for example, `record_lock_wait_s = 45` with `acquire_timeout_s = 30` can take about 60 seconds), so the new knob does not keep its stated contract and can hang a finished record longer than configured.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/hand_approve.py:_append_outcome

chunk_findings.detail: The contention hook fails the first nonzero-timeout `file_lock` call anywhere and only records a global boolean. It never checks that `lock` is the events/append lock or that the failing call is the one made by `hand_approve.record`'s append. If `AG.record` acquires another nonzero-timeout lock before the events append (for example a task-state lock), the wrapper raises there, `timed_out["done"]` becomes true, and if that unrelated lock is retried or handled the assertions at lines 44-47 can still pass even though the events append never timed out and the retry under test was never exercised. The test therefore can be vacuous for the named bug.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_gate_record_lock_retry.py:31-37

chunk_findings.detail: The test does not exercise the new `[lease].record_lock_wait_s` knob or the stated bound. It leaves config at defaults and injects exactly one lock timeout, asserting only that the outcome is recorded. A regression that ignores `record_lock_wait_s`, uses a hardcoded retry/wait, or retries unbounded passes unchanged. Given the change adds `lease.py` and `knob_added.lease.record_lock_wait_s.toml` and the docstring promises a bounded wait, the regression test must set/inspect the knob (e.g., show that total wait is bounded or that the knob value is passed to the retry loop).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_gate_record_lock_retry.py:22-48

chunk_findings.detail: The “stdlib-only decision” section states that “Completing needs no required third-party dependency,” but two lines later says that without the optional `argcomplete` extra “there is no TAB completion.” For a user who installs `ddflow` without the `argcomplete` extra and follows the activation instructions, TAB completion does not work, so the blanket “completing needs no required third-party dependency” claim is false/misleading; it should be qualified to say that candidate generation is stdlib-only while shell activation/TAB completion requires the optional `argcomplete` extra.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/completion.md:55

chunk_findings.detail: The `managed_files_backup` knob is declared without a `strictest` entry, even though the change’s own conformance requirement says each knob is declared with its strictest entry and the sibling `lane_transport` knob supplies `strictest` even when its default is already the strictest value. Given a project `.ddflow/config.toml` containing `[adapters] managed_files_backup = false`, the layer resolver has no declared strictest value to force the knob back to `true`; the project value can therefore resolve into `AdaptersConfig`, `managed_files_backup(cfg)` returns `False`, and the `ManagedFile` adapter can write shared files without the required one-time `.ddflow-bak`, violating the stated “backup on (true, not loosenable by a project layer)” policy.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/adapters.py:55 (AdaptersConfig.managed_files_backup)

chunk_findings.detail: `selected_platform` can return an unavailable adapter as the selected one. With the default `platform = "auto"` on an unsupported non-POSIX OS (for example `os.name == "java"`), the condition on line 37 is false and the function returns `Windows()` on line 39. The function’s own docstring says `Windows` is unavailable on an unsupported OS, and the code never checks adapter availability before returning it. A caller that asks this module for the platform adapter therefore receives an unavailable adapter and may proceed as if it passed selection, contrary to the acceptance rule that an unavailable adapter never reads as passed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adapters.py:39

chunk_findings.detail: The manifest declares the new `adapters.platform` knob’s value/default as `"auto"`, but the acceptance test added by this change is named `test_defaults_are_posix_local_empty_and_backup_on`, i.e. it asserts the default platform selector is `posix`. Those two declarations cannot both be correct: if `AdaptersConfig.platform` defaults to `posix`, this upgrade manifest misstates the default and users/doctor/`config --explain` will report `auto`; if the code default is actually `auto`, the added default test fails. Either way the knob’s declared default is inconsistent with the acceptance path that is supposed to read it back.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/knob_added.adapters.platform.toml:6

chunk_findings.detail: The manifest classifies the new `adapters.network_consent` knob as `impact = "additive"`, but its own `why` says a kind with no recorded consent “reads as declined” and the default is `{}`. For an existing project that already has a network-backed adapter enabled but has no `[adapters.network_consent]` table, after this upgrade `network_consented("forge")` (or any other kind) returns false and outbound network calls are refused. That is a behavior break for existing network adapter use, not an additive change, so the upgrade manifest will suppress the breaking-change notice users need.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/knob_added.adapters.network_consent.toml:8

chunk_findings.detail: The manifest classifies `adapters.managed_files_consent` as `impact = "additive"`, but its default `{}` means every managed-file kind is unconsented and the `why` says such writes are “refused, never silently written”. Given an existing project that already uses the `ManagedFile` adapter to merge `settings.json`, `.mcp.json`, `opencode.json`, `hooks.toml`, or `AGENTS.md`/`README` regions without a consent table, this upgrade changes working writes into refused writes until consent is added. That is a breaking behavior change, not an additive one.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/knob_added.adapters.managed_files_consent.toml:8

chunk_findings.detail: The test name and the unknown-value fallback in this file state that the `platform` default/strictest value is `posix`, but the test asserts `Config().adapters.platform == "auto"`. If the declared default is the `posix` value named by the acceptance, the test fails for the default `Config`; if the implementation default is `auto`, the test passes while not enforcing the stated default. In either case the acceptance is self-contradictory and can hide a wrong default for `platform`.
chunk_findings.title: `test_defaults_are_posix_local_empty_and_backup_on`

chunk_findings.detail: The `platform = "auto"` case asserts that the selected class name is `Posix` with the comment “this host is POSIX”. On a non-POSIX test host, `auto` should not resolve to `Posix`, so the test fails purely because of the execution environment. A portable test would skip on non-POSIX hosts or assert the actual auto-selected platform rather than hard-coding `Posix`.
chunk_findings.title: `test_platform_selector_reads_back_through_services_adapters`

chunk_findings.detail: `ACCEPTANCE` defines a table of knob/value/read-back triples but is never used by any test in the file. The acceptance matrix is therefore dead: changing a value or expected read-back in that table cannot cause a test failure, so it does not actually exercise the cases it lists.
chunk_findings.title: `ACCEPTANCE`

chunk_findings.detail: `stored_boot` promises to return `""` when no boot id was recorded and `observe_boot` promises that reading never raises, but it catches only `OSError`. If `.ddflow/local/boot` exists and contains invalid UTF-8 bytes, e.g. `b"\xff"`, then `Path.read_text("utf-8")` raises `UnicodeDecodeError`, which is not caught. In that state `observe_boot(repo)` propagates the exception and crashes the health pass instead of returning a result with `changed=False`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/worktree/_boot.py:34-39

chunk_findings.detail: `observe_boot` conflates an unreadable previous marker with a missing one. If the marker file already contains the current boot id but is read-denied while still writable, e.g. file mode `0222`, then `stored_boot` catches `PermissionError` and returns `""`; with a readable current boot id this makes `cur != prev`, so `observe_boot` writes the marker and returns `changed=True` even though no reboot occurred. That can license a post-reboot recovery sweep from an unchanged/unknown previous state, violating the module’s stated “unknown is not no” / never-run-an-unlicensed-sweep requirement.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/worktree/_boot.py:52

chunk_findings.detail: The new recovery kinds are resolved through the same generic mode loop as correction kinds, so a global mode override can make them `apply`. For example, with `override="apply"` (e.g. `ddflow health --mode apply`) or `[health].mode=apply`, `own.get(k, "inherit")` returns `"inherit"` for `LAPSED_ALIVE`, `READY_TO_LAND`, and `MERGE_INTERRUPTED`, and the loop returns `"apply"` for those keys. The added comment states these detectors have no apply correction and “never apply anything”; returning `apply` for them routes the health engine down an apply path for a detector that has no correction (or records it as applied) without `recover` performing the recovery.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/healthwatch.py:_modes

chunk_findings.detail: The `landed_unlogged` detector uses “branch head is an ancestor of `base`, and `base` has commits beyond the branch” as proof that a merge landed without being logged. That shape is also exactly what an empty or stale branch has. For example, an item has `branch = "feature/x"` created from `main` at commit `A`, but no commits have been added to `feature/x`; `main` then advances to commit `B`. `_merges` runs `rev-parse refs/heads/feature/x` and gets `A`, `merge-base --is-ancestor A main` succeeds, and `rev-list --count refs/heads/feature/x..main` returns `1`, so it appends `MergeHang(... landed_unlogged=True)`. This is wrong: `rev-list --count main..feature/x` is `0`, no work landed, and the branch is merely an empty/stale branch created from a commit already contained in `main`. The code never checks the empty-branch condition its comment says it excludes, so ordinary branches created from an older base, reset to base, or otherwise having no unique commits can be misreported as landed-unlogged merge hangs.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/healthwatch.py:_merges

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to verify that a lane owing more than `merge` is not proposed to land, but it never calls `H.inspect` and only asserts that the constructed `Ready` object's `owed` attribute is truthy. For the input `H.Ready("T1", "a", commits_ahead=1, owed=("unit_tests", "merge"))`, the assertion passes even if `H.inspect` returns a `ready_to_land` finding for that item, so the test cannot catch a regression that incorrectly proposes landing when work remains beyond merge.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_recovery_detectors.py:TestReadyToLand.test_more_than_merge_owed_is_not_ready_to_land

chunk_findings.detail: The added `order_pin` contract is self-contradictory. It says pins are merged tighten-only, “a layer’s keys lead and no layer removes a lower layer’s pin,” but also claims “so a company floor can keep `bugs_first` first.” If company config sets `schedule.order_pin = ["bugs_first"]` and a user/local layer above it sets `schedule.order_pin = ["critical_path"]`, the first clause puts the higher layer’s pin ahead while the second clause preserves the company pin, yielding an effective order beginning `["critical_path", "bugs_first", ...]`. Thus the company floor does not keep `bugs_first` first. The same claim in `ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/knob_added.schedule.order_pin.toml:6` repeats this incorrect guarantee.
chunk_findings.title: docs/guide/parallelism.md:313

chunk_findings.detail: The parametrized case `(["id", "priority"], "id")` does not actually test that an order with `id` not last is rejected. The assertion is `assert words in msg and "bugs_first" in msg and "critical_path" in msg`, where `words` is `"id"`. Because `id` is itself one of the known keys that the test requires to be named, any `ValueError` listing the known keys satisfies this case, even if the error has nothing to do with `id` being last. For example, if `Config.check` raised `ValueError("unknown order key: priority; known keys: bugs_first, critical_path, id")` for `["id", "priority"]`, the test would pass while the intended id-last validation was absent or wrong.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_schedule_order_knob.py:test_a_bad_order_is_refused_naming_the_known_keys

chunk_findings.detail: `managed_files_backup` is declared as an ordinary boolean knob with no `strictest` entry, even though its own doc and the intent say that `true` is the strict/backup-on value and that a project layer must not loosen it. For example, an org layer may set `[adapters] managed_files_backup = true`, while a project `.ddflow/config.toml` sets `[adapters] managed_files_backup = false`. Because the knob declaration does not mark `true` as the strict value, the layer resolver has no declared basis to keep the org value, so the project value can win and shared files will be written without the promised `.ddflow-bak`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/adapters.py:54

chunk_findings.detail: `network_consent` and `managed_files_consent` are declared as free-form `Mapping[str, bool]` knobs without `choices` or `strictest` entries, violating the conformance requirement that every knob declare its choices/outward/strictest metadata and that unrecognised values warn and fall back to the strictest default. Concretely, a project can write `[adapters.managed_files_consent]` with a kind that is unrecognised or that an org layer forbids (e.g. `"settings.json" = true`), and the registry/doctor has no declared choice/strictest information to reject, warn, or resolve the stricter org value; the consent can therefore be read as granted where the intended strict behavior is declined.

chunk_findings.detail: The `managed_files_backup` knob is declared without a `strictest` entry, even though the change’s own conformance requirement says each knob is declared with its strictest entry and the sibling `lane_transport` knob supplies `strictest` even when its default is already the strictest value. chunk_findings.detail: `selected_platform` can return an unavailable adapter as the selected one. With the default `platform = "auto"` on an unsupported non-POSIX OS (for example `os.name == "java"`), the condition on line 37 is false and the function returns `Windows()` on line 39. The function’s own docstring says `Windows` is unavailable on an unsupported OS, and the code never checks adapter availability before returning it. A caller that asks this module for the platform adapter therefore receives an unavailable adapter and may proceed as if it passed selection, contrary to the acceptance rule that an unavailable adapter never reads as passed.

chunk_findings.detail: The manifest declares the new `adapters.platform` knob’s value/default as `"auto"`, but the acceptance test added by this change is named `test_defaults_are_posix_local_empty_and_backup_on`, i.e. it asserts the default platform selector is `posix`. Those two declarations cannot both be correct: if `AdaptersConfig.platform` defaults to `posix`, this upgrade manifest misstates the default and users/doctor/`config --explain` will report `auto`; if the code default is actually `auto`, the added default test fails. Either way the knob’s declared default is inconsistent with the acceptance path that is supposed to read it back.

chunk_findings.detail: The manifest classifies the new `adapters.network_consent` knob as `impact = "additive"`, but its own `why` says a kind with no recorded consent “reads as declined” and the default is `{}`. For an existing project that already has a network-backed adapter enabled but has no `[adapters.network_consent]` table, after this upgrade `network_consented("forge")` (or any other kind) returns false and outbound network calls are refused. That is a behavior break for existing network adapter use, not an additive change, so the upgrade manifest will suppress the breaking-change notice users need.
